questions.stem: What does CLZ-160's local state connect?

options.A: azurerm_resource_group.lab to its actual Azure object ID.
options.B: A provider version to its package checksum.
options.C: A subnet name to its packet-filter priorities.
options.D: Every subscription to one Terraform tenant.

optionExplanations.A: State maps configuration addresses to managed objects.
optionExplanations.B: Provider dependency checksums belong to the dependency lock file.
optionExplanations.C: There is no subnet or NSG in this lesson; state records the managed group.
optionExplanations.D: State does not merge identity boundaries.

questions.stem: Which backend pattern does the supplied CLZ-160 lesson use?

options.A: A required Azure blob backend already deployed here.
options.B: Local terraform.tfstate in its working context.
options.C: State embedded in README.md.
options.D: Browser localStorage as Terraform state.

optionExplanations.A: No storage account/backend is declared here.
optionExplanations.B: Remote Azure Storage is introduced later.
optionExplanations.C: Markdown is not the backend.
optionExplanations.D: Learner progress is not infrastructure state.

questions.stem: Which command checks the state inventory without deleting bindings?

options.A: terraform state rm azurerm_resource_group.lab
options.B: terraform destroy
options.C: terraform state list
options.D: Remove-Item terraform.tfstate

optionExplanations.A: That removes a binding.
optionExplanations.B: That proposes removal of resources.
optionExplanations.C: It lists resource addresses.
optionExplanations.D: That deletes a local artifact and loses tracking.

questions.stem: Which command shows this lesson's stored resource-group attributes?

options.A: terraform output azurerm_resource_group.lab
options.B: az account clear
options.C: terraform fmt -check
options.D: terraform state show azurerm_resource_group.lab

optionExplanations.A: Output takes an output name, not this address.
optionExplanations.B: That clears CLI account cache.
optionExplanations.C: That checks source formatting.
optionExplanations.D: It inspects the specified managed address.

questions.stem: Why compare terraform state show with az group show?

options.A: To confirm both describe the same Azure resource.
options.B: To prove every tag is a secret.
options.C: To increase the group quota.
options.D: To migrate the backend automatically.

optionExplanations.A: The Azure ID ties state ownership to the live object.
optionExplanations.B: Tags are not inherently secrets.
optionExplanations.C: Inspection does not raise quotas.
optionExplanations.D: These reads do not migrate state.

sources.title: Manage resource groups with Azure CLI

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a state lock during a state-changing operation?

options.A: Guarantee that nobody can read the file.
options.B: Prevent concurrent writers from corrupting or conflicting over state.
options.C: Prevent all Azure Portal changes forever.
options.D: Pin provider package versions.

optionExplanations.A: Locks are not access-control encryption.
optionExplanations.B: Locking protects a shared state context.
optionExplanations.C: Backend locks do not lock every Azure operation.
optionExplanations.D: The dependency lock file serves that purpose.

questions.stem: A second terminal cannot obtain a local state lock while the first Terraform operation is running. What should happen?

options.A: Delete the lock and run both applies.
options.B: Edit both state files simultaneously.
options.C: Wait for or safely stop the active operation.
options.D: Rename the resource group in Azure.

optionExplanations.A: That risks competing writes.
optionExplanations.B: Manual concurrent editing is unsafe.
optionExplanations.C: Do not remove protection while another writer is active.
optionExplanations.D: That does not resolve the active writer.

questions.stem: When is force-unlock appropriate for a backend that supports it?

options.A: Whenever a plan takes longer than expected.
options.B: Before every apply.
options.C: To unlock another active local process's state.
options.D: Only after proving the lock is stale and no writer remains.

optionExplanations.A: A long operation may still be active.
optionExplanations.B: That removes normal locking protection.
optionExplanations.C: Local state held by another process cannot be safely cleared this way.
optionExplanations.D: It is a recovery action, not routine contention handling.

questions.stem: terraform.tfstate was deleted but the Azure group still exists. What is the safe recovery approach?

options.A: Restore a known backup or import the known object.
options.B: Assume the group was deleted too.
options.C: Create a new group with the same name blindly.
options.D: Write an invented Azure ID into JSON.

optionExplanations.A: Recover the binding before managing its lifecycle.
optionExplanations.B: Deleting state does not delete Azure resources.
optionExplanations.C: That can collide with the existing object.
optionExplanations.D: Manual fabricated state is unsafe.

questions.stem: What does terraform state rm do to a managed object's binding?

options.A: Delete the Azure object automatically.
options.B: Remove the state record while leaving the remote object.
options.C: Rotate every resource password.
options.D: Encrypt the remaining state.

optionExplanations.A: State removal is not cloud deletion.
optionExplanations.B: It makes Terraform stop tracking that object.
optionExplanations.C: It does not perform credential rotation.
optionExplanations.D: It is not an encryption command.

questions.stem: Why restrict access to Terraform state even when source marks outputs sensitive?

options.A: Sensitive always means the value is absent from state.
options.B: Only the state filename can reveal data.
options.C: State can still contain sensitive values.
options.D: Public state is required for provider verification.

optionExplanations.A: That is false for ordinary sensitive values.
optionExplanations.B: The contents also matter.
optionExplanations.C: Display redaction does not remove stored data.
optionExplanations.D: Provider verification does not require publishing state.

questions.stem: Which result should git status show for state, saved plans, and .terraform runtime files?

options.A: All must be added to the public repository.
options.B: Only state should be committed.
options.C: Plans should be committed because they only contain change counts.
options.D: They should not appear as tracked lesson source.

optionExplanations.A: They can contain sensitive or machine-specific data.
optionExplanations.B: State should remain protected outside Git.
optionExplanations.C: Plans can include full values and sensitive data.
optionExplanations.D: The lesson expects generated runtime data excluded.

questions.stem: What should remain committed after CLZ-160 cleanup?

options.A: The provider dependency lock file.
options.B: The live terraform.tfstate containing secrets.
options.C: A manually cleared state-lock marker.
options.D: The latest binary tfplan.

optionExplanations.A: It preserves reviewed dependencies.
optionExplanations.B: State is excluded from source control.
optionExplanations.C: Transient locking data is not committed configuration.
optionExplanations.D: Plans are generated operational artifacts.

questions.stem: Azure tags were changed outside Terraform. What should the learner run to inspect the resulting difference?

options.A: Edit terraform.tfstate by hand.
options.B: terraform plan
options.C: terraform fmt alone.
options.D: Rename the README.

optionExplanations.A: The lesson explicitly avoids manual state edits.
optionExplanations.B: Normal planning reads live objects and proposes reconciliation.
optionExplanations.C: Formatting does not refresh Azure attributes.
optionExplanations.D: Documentation names do not refresh infrastructure.

questions.stem: Why use only CLZ-160's folder for its apply and destroy?

options.A: Azure authenticates based only on folder names.
options.B: All folders must have identical state.
options.C: It holds this lesson's configuration and state context.
options.D: The region prohibits commands from other paths.

optionExplanations.A: Authentication comes from identity context.
optionExplanations.B: Independent lessons have separate contexts.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong context can target unrelated managed objects.
optionExplanations.D: Azure does not enforce repository paths.

questions.stem: In azurerm_resource_group.lab, what does lab identify?

options.A: The Azure region.
options.B: The user's tenant.
options.C: The backend password.
options.D: The local resource name in Terraform configuration.

optionExplanations.A: Location is a separate attribute.
optionExplanations.B: Identity context is separate.
optionExplanations.C: It is not a credential.
optionExplanations.D: It is part of the address, not necessarily the Azure group's name.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes configuration from state?

options.A: Configuration expresses intent; state records managed bindings and attributes.
options.B: State replaces the need for source code.
options.C: Configuration lists every live Azure object automatically.
options.D: State is only a formatting cache.

optionExplanations.A: Both are used to determine lifecycle actions.
optionExplanations.B: Intent remains in configuration.
optionExplanations.C: Only declared/imported management is represented.
optionExplanations.D: It contains operational object data.

questions.stem: terraform show -json returns state values for PowerShell inspection. What kind of operation is that?

options.A: Automatic resource recreation.
options.B: Read-only serialization of the selected Terraform data.
options.C: An Azure RBAC grant.
options.D: A remote-backend migration.

optionExplanations.A: Show is inspection.
optionExplanations.B: It does not apply Azure changes.
optionExplanations.C: Serialization grants no access.
optionExplanations.D: No init migration is invoked.

questions.stem: After destroy, state is empty but az group exists returns true. What should the learner conclude?

options.A: Empty state proves Azure must be wrong.
options.B: The group is free and may always be ignored.
options.C: Cleanup is not independently confirmed.
options.D: Terraform automatically owns all remaining resources.

optionExplanations.A: State absence cannot overrule live existence.
optionExplanations.B: Ownership and cleanup still need resolution.
optionExplanations.C: Azure still reports the named group in that context.
optionExplanations.D: Bindings are not inferred from every Azure object.

sources.title: Manage resource groups with Azure CLI

questions.stem: Why separate production state by environment?

options.A: Because Terraform cannot store more than one resource.
options.B: Because dev tags automatically encrypt data.
options.C: To make every resource globally anonymous.
options.D: To reduce accidental cross-environment management and access.

optionExplanations.A: State can contain multiple resources.
optionExplanations.B: Tags are not encryption.
optionExplanations.C: Environment separation is not anonymization.
optionExplanations.D: Different environments need distinct ownership contexts.

questions.stem: An Azure object exists, but the current state inventory is empty because a local file was lost. Why not assume destroy will find it?

options.A: Destroy acts on managed state bindings.
options.B: Destroy scans all subscriptions automatically.
options.C: Azure names are universal Terraform addresses.
options.D: Terraform infers ownership from the Lab tag automatically.

optionExplanations.A: Recover or import before state-driven cleanup.
optionExplanations.B: It does not discover and delete all Azure objects.
optionExplanations.C: A name is not a recovered binding.
optionExplanations.D: A tag does not reconstruct a missing state binding.

questions.stem: A user suggests -lock=false to bypass another teammate's backend operation. What is the safer choice?

options.A: Always bypass because plans are cheap.
options.B: Resolve the contention instead of disabling the lock.
options.C: Copy the state into a public issue.
options.D: Delete the teammate's resources.

optionExplanations.A: Cost does not remove concurrency risk.
optionExplanations.B: Concurrent changes can conflict over the same state.
optionExplanations.C: That can expose sensitive data.
optionExplanations.D: That is unrelated and destructive.

questions.stem: Changing backend storage location is conceptually different from changing which Azure group?

options.A: The backend is always the resource group itself.
options.B: Moving state always deletes the subscription.
options.C: The backend stores tracking data; resources remain separately managed.
options.D: Backends only store README text.

optionExplanations.A: The group is a managed object, not local storage.
optionExplanations.B: Migration does not imply subscription deletion.
optionExplanations.C: A migration need not rename or recreate the object.
optionExplanations.D: They store Terraform operational state.

questions.stem: Which production control fits the lesson's remote-state guidance?

options.A: A publicly readable blob with no versioning.
options.B: A shared state file emailed to everyone.
options.C: Only a renamed state file.
options.D: Restricted Azure AD authorization and recovery controls.

optionExplanations.A: That exposes data and weakens recovery.
optionExplanations.B: That loses centralized access/concurrency controls.
optionExplanations.C: Obscure naming is not authorization.
optionExplanations.D: State readers and writers need deliberate access.

questions.stem: Does CLZ-160's local lock coordinate independent copied state files on two different workstations?

options.A: No; each copy can become an independent management context.
options.B: Yes; local files communicate automatically.
options.C: Only if both folders have the same name.
options.D: Only if both copies use the same Azure credentials.

optionExplanations.A: Use an appropriate shared backend for team coordination.
optionExplanations.B: No such remote coordination is configured.
optionExplanations.C: Names do not create a shared backend.
optionExplanations.D: Matching credentials do not make independent local state files share a lock.

questions.stem: What should exist in configuration before importing a known lost resource binding?

options.A: An arbitrary output named import.
options.B: The intended resource block and correct ownership context.
options.C: A publicly posted access token.
options.D: A deleted subscription.

optionExplanations.A: Outputs do not define resource ownership.
optionExplanations.B: Import records the object under a chosen configuration address.
optionExplanations.C: Authentication secrets should remain private.
optionExplanations.D: Import needs access to the actual object.

questions.stem: terraform state list shows one resource group. Does that mean the Azure subscription has only one group?

options.A: Yes; state lists every accessible object.
options.B: Only if environment=dev.
options.C: No; it lists this state context's managed addresses.
options.D: Yes, because AzureRM is installed.

optionExplanations.A: Terraform state is scoped to managed bindings.
optionExplanations.B: Environment values do not expand inventory.
optionExplanations.C: It is not a complete subscription inventory.
optionExplanations.D: A plugin does not imply discovery of all objects.

questions.stem: Why should a Terraform state backup receive similar protection as the current state?

options.A: Backups always contain only file dates.
options.B: Backups are automatically public-safe.
options.C: Backup names grant encryption.
options.D: It may retain the same sensitive operational data.

optionExplanations.A: They can hold complete prior state.
optionExplanations.B: No such guarantee exists.
optionExplanations.C: Filenames do not encrypt contents.
optionExplanations.D: Older copies can still contain credentials and resource attributes.

questions.stem: Which result should successful CLZ-160 cleanup leave in the managed inventory?

options.A: No managed resource addresses.
options.B: A phantom address for every old tag.
options.C: A stored VM password.
options.D: The old group as still managed and running.

optionExplanations.A: The group binding is removed after deletion.
optionExplanations.B: Tags are attributes, not standalone resource addresses.
optionExplanations.C: This lesson creates no VM password.
optionExplanations.D: That contradicts successful destruction.

questions.stem: How should two terminals demonstrate locking without defeating it?

options.A: Force-unlock as soon as the second terminal waits.
options.B: Observe contention during a state-changing operation and let the owner finish.
options.C: Manually edit JSON in both terminals.
options.D: Delete all lock files while applying.

optionExplanations.A: That may disrupt an active writer.
optionExplanations.B: The exercise is about protection, not concurrent bypass.
optionExplanations.C: That does not safely exercise Terraform locking.
optionExplanations.D: That risks state integrity.
